analysis.one_liner: Requires employers with 15 or more workers to let employees earn up to seven paid sick days a year.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate HELP Committee in May 2011 and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or floor action before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require employers with 15 or more employees to let workers earn one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, capped at 56 hours (about seven workdays) a year. Workers could use the time for their own illness or medical care, to care for a sick child, spouse, parent, or similar family member, and to deal with domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking — including medical care, counseling, relocation, and court proceedings. The bill was introduced by Senator Tom Harkin of Iowa in May 2011 and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it stayed until the Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 40 million private-sector workers who lacked any paid sick time when the bill was introduced, plus millions more who could not use their existing time to care for a sick family member. The bill's own findings note that 68 percent of private-sector workers in the lowest earnings quartile lacked paid sick time, so the gains would flow heavily to low-wage workers — disproportionately women, who bear most family caregiving — and to victims of domestic violence who risk losing a job when they take time to seek help.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-wage workers without paid sick time

how_it_helps.text: Employers with 15 or more employees must let each worker earn at least one hour of paid sick time per 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours per calendar year, usable for their own medical needs, care for family members, and time related to domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking.

Workers begin earning the time at hire and can use it starting on the 60th day; unused time carries over year to year, and employers cannot require workers to find a replacement as a condition of taking the time.

Employers are barred from firing, disciplining, or retaliating against workers who use the time, including counting the absences under no-fault attendance policies, and the Labor Secretary gets enforcement authority modeled on existing wage-and-hour law.
Employers that already offer an equivalent paid leave policy usable for the same purposes do not have to add anything, and nothing in the bill prevents more generous policies.

analysis.who_pays: Employers of 15 or more people — including public agencies — would bear the cost of paid time off that was not previously provided, most heavily in low-wage industries such as retail, food service, and hospitality where paid sick time was least common. Some workers would also face the cost of getting a health care provider's certification for absences longer than three consecutive days, a burden the bill directs regulators to address for people without health insurance.

drawbacks.text: The mandate is a real cost for employers, concentrated in businesses with many low-wage and part-time workers who currently get no paid sick time; the bill acknowledges the feasibility concern by capping the requirement at 56 hours a year and excusing employers with equivalent existing policies.

Employers may require a health care provider's certification for any absence longer than three consecutive workdays, which can impose a cost and a delay on workers — the bill specifically requires regulations to spell out how workers without health insurance can meet this requirement, an implicit acknowledgment of that burden.

Earned time does not have to be paid out if a worker quits or is fired, and covered employers can hold workers to the 56-hour carryover cap, limiting the benefit to about seven days a year rather than an open-ended entitlement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to workers is modest but real and targeted: about seven paid days a year, capped, with an exemption for employers who already offer equivalent leave. The main honest cost falls on employers in low-wage industries that currently provide no sick time, and a smaller burden comes from doctor's-note requirements for longer absences. The bill is structured to phase in over collective bargaining agreements and to leave state laws that are more generous untouched. On balance it is a straightforward transfer of a modest new benefit to workers at a modest, predictable cost to employers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or floor action in the Senate or the House before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Harkin of Iowa introduced the Healthy Families Act on May 12, 2011, joined by 18 cosponsors — 17 Democrats and one Independent — who were listed as original co-introducers.
The same day it was introduced, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action — no hearing, no committee report, no Senate vote, and no House action — appears in the complete action history before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

The bill's findings state that nearly 40 percent of the private-sector workforce, about 40 million workers, lacked paid sick time at the time, and that 68 percent of private-sector workers in the lowest earnings quartile lacked it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have been required to provide paid sick time, particularly in retail, food service, and other low-wage industries, are better off because the bill never advanced, and the roughly 40 million workers who would have gained paid sick days remain without it.

for.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Iowa (bill sponsor; chair of the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Healthy Families Act and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: 18 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Joined as original co-introducers of the bill on the day of introduction.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral in the Democratic-controlled Senate
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on May 12, 2011 and never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote in the entire Congress.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority party in the House of Representatives during the 112th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought any version of the bill to the House floor; no House action on the bill appears in the record.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and business lobbies
against.role: Business trade groups opposing paid sick leave mandates
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal paid sick leave requirements as a cost burden on employers, contributing to an environment in which the bill never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or Independent; no Republican signed on, and the bill moved nowhere in a Senate committee its own sponsor chaired and a Republican-controlled House never considered it.

industries.industry: Retail, food service, hospitality, and other low-wage employers
industries.note: These employers would bear the direct cost of providing paid sick time where little exists today — the bill's own findings show 68 percent of the lowest-paid quartile of workers lacked it. The cost to them is the benefit to their workers, so their interest runs against the people the bill serves.

industries.industry: Large employers with existing paid leave policies
industries.note: Employers already offering an equivalent paid leave policy usable for the same purposes are exempt from any new obligation, so the bill largely ratifies rather than extends their existing practice.

industries.industry: Health care providers and the health care sector
industries.note: The bill's findings argue that paid sick time lets workers get routine and preventive care and reduces the spread of contagious disease, which would channel more patients into regular care instead of emergency rooms; workers and providers benefit together, at employers' expense.
